history.heading: A medieval co-principality
paragraphs: Andorra lies high in the eastern Pyrenees between France and Spain. According to tradition, Charlemagne granted the Andorrans a charter in the 9th century in return for fighting the Moors. The territory later came under the Counts of Urgell and then the Bishop of Urgell.

Disputes between the Bishop of Urgell and the French Counts of Foix were settled by the paréages of 1278 and 1288, which established shared sovereignty. The rights of the Counts of Foix later passed to the kings of France and eventually to the president of France.

history.heading: Isolation and modernisation
paragraphs: For centuries Andorra was a poor and isolated mountain community of shepherds and farmers, which kept its independence partly because of its remoteness. Its traditional institutions, including the General Council of the Valleys founded in 1419, are among the oldest parliaments in Europe.

From the mid-20th century, roads, tourism and duty-free trade transformed the country. Andorra adopted its first written constitution in 1993, becoming a parliamentary democracy, and joined the United Nations the same year.

culture.heading: Language and traditions
paragraphs: Catalan is the official language, and Andorra is the only country where it has this status. Spanish, Portuguese and French are also widely spoken, as a large share of residents are foreign-born.
Most of the population is Roman Catholic, and the country has many Romanesque churches. Traditional dances such as the contrapàs and the sardana are performed at village festivals.

culture.heading: Mountain life
paragraphs: The Madriu-Perafita-Claror Valley, a glacial valley with shepherds' huts and terraced fields, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Local dishes include escudella (a hearty stew), trinxat (cabbage and potato) and mountain cheeses and cured meats.
Skiing, hiking and mountain biking are central to both local life and tourism.

politics.heading: Two co-princes
paragraphs: Andorra is a parliamentary co-principality. Its heads of state are two co-princes: the Bishop of Urgell in Spain and the President of France, who hold mostly ceremonial roles.
Legislative power belongs to the General Council, which elects the head of government. The country's seven parishes have considerable local autonomy.

politics.heading: Relations with Europe
paragraphs: Andorra is not a member of the European Union, but it uses the euro under a monetary agreement and has a customs union with the EU for industrial goods. It has negotiated an association agreement with the EU to deepen access to the single market.

economy.heading: Tourism and services
paragraphs: Tourism dominates the economy, with millions of visitors each year coming for skiing in winter, hiking in summer and shopping. Low taxes on goods such as tobacco, alcohol and electronics attract shoppers from France and Spain.

Banking is also important. Andorra was long considered a tax haven, but it introduced income and corporate taxes in the 2010s and agreed to share financial information with other countries. A shortage of affordable housing is a major concern.
